A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Layered Diffusion Brushes work. Text, equations, figures, and results are readable, including v2's complete supplementary material. Retained content can be matched despite extensive rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports an original seven-participant comparative user study, SUS and creativity-support results, edited-image examples, and qualitative parameter analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains the user-study results and adds quantitative benchmark comparisons, timestep ablations, and original overlapping-edit and video-editing examples.

M1.justification: v1 describes a shared regeneration latent and blending with the preceding layer. v2 Sections 3.3–3.3.1 add per-layer inversion of the preceding edited image, caching of its regeneration and blending states, and recursive updates for overlapping edits. The video extension also applies caching across SVD frames. These extend the procedure while retaining the single-layer masked-noise and late-blending core.

E1.justification: v2 adds PIE-Bench image-editing evaluation and multilayer editing of SVD-generated videos, introducing temporal consistency requirements beyond v1's still-image tasks. The generated-image/freeform tasks and MagicBrush real-image user study remain.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates Blended Latent Diffusion, HD-Painter, and BrushNet alongside InstructPix2Pix and Stable Diffusion Inpainting in MagicBrush comparisons and the new quantitative evaluation. v1 discussed some related methods but its main reported comparison evaluated only InstructPix2Pix and Stable Diffusion Inpainting.

E3.justification: v2 introduces eight image-quality, preservation, and text-alignment metrics, plus a timing protocol using 25 diffusion steps for baselines and eight editing steps for LDB. MagicBrush comparisons mix user-edited LDB/IP2P/SDI outputs with default-setting outputs from other methods. These are substantial new evaluation protocols; the retained user study does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v1's qualitative strength/step-count grid is expanded into quantitative regeneration-step analysis and a new systematic blending-step ablation, with qualitative examples and metric curves in v2 Figures 6–7 and 13–14. The regeneration analysis extends the earlier step-count analysis, and the strength example survives as Figure 12. Figure 3 additionally demonstrates interacting, overlapping edits.

E5.justification: The participant-response distributions are retained. Neither version supplies repeated-run or seed-count reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for model comparisons. v2's new metric curves report point estimates without uncertainty bands.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1 adds extensive numerical comparisons, including LDB timings of 0.26 seconds on MagicBrush and 0.25 seconds on PIE-Bench under its eight-step protocol, alongside new ablation findings and qualitative examples. These are new measurements, not a same-setting deterioration from the retained 140 ms claim. SUS scores remain 80.35 for LDB, 38.21 for IP2P, and 37.5 for SDI.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal layer-state tuple and a latent-generation dependency map in Equations 1–2, including visibility and predecessor-layer information absent from v1's formalization. No theorem or proof is added. The brush-strength scaling equation is retained with revised notation.

C1.justification: v2 broadens the central claims from real-time editing and usability against two tools to quantitative state-of-the-art speed and quality comparisons, including a claimed 53-fold speed advantage over BrushNet. It explicitly claims independence for overlapping edits and demonstrates applicability to video. The underlying training-free editing and 140 ms claims already appear in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of regeneration/blending trade-offs, arguments about temporal coherence and broader model applicability, and an explicit limitation concerning semantically implausible edits. Earlier user-feedback caveats largely survive in the supplement. The new quantitative discussion incorrectly calls 86.02 an HPS score; Table 1 assigns it to scaled Image Reward.

D1.justification: v2 identifies RTX 4090 hardware, adds a caching-memory estimate and project-page link, and associates the 140 ms example with four editing steps. The study description newly reports five editing steps where v1 documented 13 generation steps; these describe different operations and do not establish a 13-to-five budget reduction. Most existing implementation and study details move to the supplement.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning through a dedicated caching subsection covering DeepCache, AdaCache, block caching, and approximate caching. It also develops comparisons with newer layered/sequential editing and inpainting work, including LayeringDiff, ParallelEdits, MAG-Edit, and BrushNet. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and discussion are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around caching, editing, and layer formulation, while much UI documentation, study procedure, questionnaires, and interview discussion move into supplementary sections. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to show the cache bank and layer feedback. v2 adds a quantitative comparison table, overlapping-edit and video illustrations, expanded comparison grids, and quantitative ablation plots. Existing UI screenshots and SUS/CSI charts are relocated, while the strength illustration is reformatted. The visual presentation changes substantially.

improvement.justification: Table 1, the PIE-Bench evaluation, and quantitative timestep ablations address v1's important lack of quantitative image-quality comparisons and systematic evidence for its caching choices. Clearer layer specification and broader research positioning further strengthen the paper. Unequal MagicBrush tuning conditions and the IR/HPS reporting error limit some superiority claims, but the added evidence makes the technical contribution substantially more assessable.
